subject: instrumentation-process-control
title: Response of First-Order System
aim: To study the behavior and determine the time constant of a first-order process subjected to step and sinusoidal heat input changes.
apparatus: Circulating water bath with electric heater

parts.title: Part A: Step Input Response
parts.aim: To study the behavior and to determine the time constant of a first-order process subjected to a step change in heat input (thermometer/thermocouple immersed in a heating bath).
parts.system: Changes in the temperature of a fluid due to step changes in the external heat supply.
parts.theory:
Heat transfer between the heating bath surroundings at temperature T_s and the temperature sensor (thermocouple/RTD/thermometer) at temperature T' is governed by a first-order dynamic energy balance.

Assumptions:
(i) Uniform bead temperature (no gradients in thermocouple bead)
(ii) No conduction in the leads
(iii) Constant physical properties (density, specific heat, heat transfer coefficient)
(iv) Fast sensor millivolt-to-°C conversion with zero dynamics

Energy Balance:
hA(T - T_s) = m C_p (dT'/dt)

At Steady State:
hA(T_s - T_s') = m C_p (dT_s'/dt) = 0

Introducing Deviation Variables T̄ = T - T_s and T̄' = T' - T_s':
hA(T̄ - T̄') = m C_p (dT̄'/dt) => T̄ - T̄' = τ (dT̄'/dt)
where τ = (m C_p) / (h A) is the time constant.

Laplace Domain Transfer Function:
T̄'(s) / T̄(s) = 1 / (τs + 1) = K e^{-Ds} / (τs + 1)

Step Response Solution:
T̄'(t) = K (1 - e^{-(t-D)/τ})
At t = τ, T̄'(τ) = 0.632 × ΔT (63.2% of total temperature rise).

formulas.label: Sensor Energy Balance
formulas.derivation: Dynamic heat transfer from bath surroundings at T_s to sensor bead at T'.
formulas.purpose: Establishes dynamic thermal equilibrium for the sensor.

formulas.label: Time Constant (τ)
formulas.derivation: Defined by grouping physical properties m C_p divided by h A.
formulas.purpose: Measures system response speed. Smaller τ means faster response.

formulas.label: Laplace Transfer Function
formulas.derivation: Transformed into s-domain using deviation variables.
formulas.purpose: Relates output deviation temperature to input step in s-domain.
assumptions: Linear first-order system with dead time

formulas.label: Time Domain Step Response
formulas.derivation: Inverse Laplace transform of unit step response.
formulas.purpose: Predicts sensor output temperature at any time t following step change.
assumptions: Pure step change in bath temperature

viva_questions.question: 1. What is the time constant? How does it affect the response of a system?
viva_questions.answer: Time constant (τ) is the time required for the system response to reach 63.2% of its ultimate final steady-state value following a step change. A smaller time constant indicates a fast, responsive system, whereas a larger time constant indicates a slow, sluggish system.

viva_questions.question: 2. Do the size of the bulb and the amount of mercury affect the response of the thermometer?
viva_questions.answer: Yes. The time constant τ = (m Cp) / (h A) depends directly on the mass of mercury (m) and surface area (A). A larger bulb contains more mercury (higher mass m), which increases heat capacity and lengthens the time constant, making response slower unless surface area A increases proportionally.

viva_questions.question: 3. What is the physical significance of steady-state gain?
viva_questions.answer: Steady-state gain (K) is the ratio of ultimate output change to input step change (ΔY / ΔX). Higher process gain means the system produces a larger output change for a given input change, making the process highly sensitive and requiring less aggressive controller action.

parts.title: Part B: Sinusoidal Input Response
parts.aim: To study the sinusoidal response of a thermowell/thermocouple in a circulating water bath to a sinusoidal (cyclic ON/OFF) heat input, and compare input vs output temperature-time curves, amplitude ratio, frequency of oscillation, time constant, phase lag, and normalized output deviation.
parts.system: Thermowell in a circulating water bath subjected to periodic cyclic heating.
parts.theory:
The dynamic response of a first-order thermal instrument to a sinusoidal temperature variation is governed by:

1) I/p amplitude = (max Bath temp - min Bath temp) / 2 = (48 - 28) / 2 = 10 °C
2) O/p amplitude = (max Thermowell - min Thermowell) / 2 = (43 - 37) / 2 = 3 °C
3) Amplitude Ratio (AR) = (O/p amplitude) / (I/p amplitude) = 3 / 10 = 0.3
4) Freq of oscillation (ω) = 2π / 60 = 0.105 rad/s
5) Time constant (τ) = √(1 - AR²) / (AR × Freq) = √(1 - 0.3²) / (0.3 × 0.1047) = 30.36 s
6) Phase lag (φ) = (observed phase lag × 360) / 60 = 60°
7) Normalized output deviation (θ/A) = 0.1365

formulas.label: i) Input Amplitude (I/p Amplitude)
formulas.derivation: Calculates half peak-to-peak amplitude of input water bath temperature oscillation.
assumptions: Symmetric cyclic heating bath temperature oscillation

formulas.label: ii) Output Amplitude (O/p Amplitude)
formulas.derivation: Calculates half peak-to-peak amplitude of output thermowell sensor temperature.

formulas.label: iii) Amplitude Ratio (AR)
formulas.derivation: Ratio of output wave amplitude to input wave amplitude.
formulas.purpose: Measures attenuation of signal (AR ≤ 1.0 for first-order lag).

formulas.label: iv) Frequency of Oscillation (ω)
formulas.derivation: Circular frequency for period T = 60 seconds.
formulas.purpose: Calculates input cycle frequency in rad/s.

formulas.label: v) Time Constant (τ)
formulas.purpose: Calculates first-order system time constant from amplitude ratio and frequency.

formulas.label: vi) Phase Lag (φ)
formulas.derivation: Converts observed peak time delay in seconds into angular degrees.
formulas.purpose: Calculates phase lag angle in degrees.

formulas.label: vii) Normalized Output Deviation (θ/A)
formulas.derivation: Ratio of indicated temperature deviation to input amplitude.

viva_questions.question: 1. What is the formula for Amplitude Ratio (AR)?
viva_questions.answer: Amplitude ratio AR = (Output Amplitude) / (Input Amplitude) = (max Thermowell - min Thermowell) / (max Bath temp - min Bath temp) = 3 / 10 = 0.3.

viva_questions.question: 2. How is time constant calculated from Amplitude Ratio?
viva_questions.answer: Time constant τ = sqrt(1 - AR^2) / (AR × Freq of oscillation) = sqrt(1 - 0.3^2) / (0.3 × 0.105) = 30.36 sec.
